strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP safety problem through substantial empirical coverage: 13 attack methods, six open and closed models, and 160 questions spanning 16 policy categories. The taxonomy and model-specific breakdowns provide a useful organizing framework.

The evaluator receives meaningful human validation: 640 responses, three annotators, Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.87, and 94.84% agreement with majority labels. Explicitly addressing refusals, paraphrases, and irrelevant harmful responses improves on simplistic string matching.

No-attack baselines, three experimental repetitions, transfer experiments, and runtime measurements provide useful descriptive evidence. Findings about competitive human-written prompts and model-dependent obfuscation performance are practically informative.
weaknesses: The comparison protocol does not establish fair attack budgets. Section 5.3 counts any successful response among 50 Generation Exploitation candidates while describing the metric as top-1. Equal numbers of prompt modifications also do not equalize target queries or computation across other methods. A fixed-decoding, 50-sample baseline and success-versus-budget comparisons are needed to isolate the benefit of decoding manipulation. Aggregate rankings additionally compare methods evaluated on different model subsets.

The success criterion does not adequately establish the claimed harmful fulfillment or policy violations. Section 5.3 describes Label C as answer correctness, whereas Figure 9 asks only whether content is directly or indirectly related to the request; Label B also accepts willingness. Provider usage restrictions are not automatically requirements to refuse every related question. Human agreement supports consistency under this rubric but does not resolve whether the rubric measures the intended safety failures.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the proposed benchmark. The manuscript provides no artifact link identifying the exact 160 questions and implementations, omits the evaluator’s three demonstrations, and does not enumerate Generation Exploitation’s 50 configurations. API model snapshots and experiment dates are unspecified. GCG uses 500 steps in Sections 5.4 and 7.1 but 50 in Table 8. These gaps, together with the measurement concerns, are decisive for the resubmission recommendation.

Baseline fidelity is questionable for Masterkey. Section 3.3 substitutes rewriting the AIM template because source code was unavailable, without demonstrating that this reproduces Masterkey’s learning procedure. Its results should be identified as an approximation or supported by implementation validation.

Several conclusions exceed the reported evidence. The claim that optimized prompts consistently perform best conflicts with AIM matching or exceeding optimized methods on several models in Table 2. Calling Llama2 unaffected by transfer overlooks AutoDAN’s 0.39 ASR versus a 0.31 baseline. Political Activities has an average attacked ASR of 0.71 versus 0.84 without attacks, illustrating why absolute compliance and incremental jailbreak success must be distinguished.

Generality and contemporary positioning need stronger qualification. Ten manually selected questions per category and transfer from Vicuna alone support a bounded study; repeated generations do not measure uncertainty over question selection. Explanations invoking model capability or training corpora remain hypotheses without controlled evidence. For ACL 2025, the comprehensive-benchmark claim also needs positioning against work such as HarmBench and JailbreakBench.
